steps.title: Hour 2: Communication & Documentation
steps.content:
WHY DOCUMENTATION MATTERS
Accurate documentation is the backbone of safe, high-quality home care. It tells the story of the visit, protects the client and the caregiver, and helps the team coordinate care.

WHAT TO DOCUMENT
Record the services you provided, client activities, significant observations, accidents or incidents, falls, changes in condition, missed or refused services, safety concerns, and communication with the office or supervisor.

DOCUMENTATION RULES
Documentation must be accurate, objective, timely, complete, and truthful. Write what you observed and did, not medical diagnoses or assumptions. Use approved abbreviations only. If you did not do it, do not document it.

COMMUNICATION WITH THE OFFICE
Stay in contact with your supervisor about scheduling, assignment concerns, client changes, and emergencies. Use the open-door policy to raise questions or suggestions without fear of reprisal.

REPORTING INCIDENTS
Report accidents, falls, suspected abuse, safety hazards, and significant changes in the client's condition immediately. Complete any required incident report within 24 hours.

PROTECTING CLIENT INFORMATION
Do not discuss clients in public, on social media, or with unauthorized people. Keep written notes secure and do not photograph client information or homes.

steps.title: Hour 2: Employment Basics & Terms of Employment
steps.content:
AT-WILL EMPLOYMENT
Employment at Golden Ages Home Care is at-will. Either you or the agency may end the employment relationship at any time. This handbook does not create a contract of employment.

OPEN DOOR POLICY
We encourage open, professional communication. You may discuss concerns about client care, safety, scheduling, workplace issues, or suggestions with your supervisor or higher management without fear of retaliation.

EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITY
Golden Ages Home Care is committed to non-discrimination and equal opportunity in hiring, training, promotion, and all employment practices. Harassment of any kind is grounds for immediate termination.

PERFORMANCE EVALUATIONS
Formal written performance evaluations are conducted at 90 days after hire and annually thereafter. Evaluations consider attendance, punctuality, quality of care, documentation, professionalism, communication, and client satisfaction.

ANNUAL TRAINING
All caregivers attend required orientation and annual in-service training such as HIPAA, infection control, abuse recognition, and emergency preparedness. Additional training may be assigned based on client needs.

LEAVES AND ACCOMMODATIONS
Medical and family leave may be available under FMLA and CFRA. Reasonable accommodations for disabilities or religious observances will be considered when they do not create an undue hardship. Discuss needs with your supervisor or HR.

steps.title: Hour 2: HIPAA & Confidentiality
steps.content:
WHAT HIPAA MEANS FOR YOU
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act protects the privacy and security of protected health information (PHI). For home care, it is all about keeping client information private.

PROTECTED HEALTH INFORMATION (PHI)
PHI includes any information created by the agency about a client, in any form: paper, electronic, photos, videos, or spoken. Individually identifiable information includes name, address, date of birth, social security number, medical record number, and photos.

MINIMUM NECESSARY RULE
Share only the minimum information needed for the task at hand, even when authorized. Do not look at records for clients you are not caring for.

CONSENT AND AUTHORIZATION
Clients sign consent for treatment, payment, and health-care operations. Authorization is required for uses outside of care. Clients have the right to access, amend, and request an accounting of disclosures.

PRACTICAL PROTECTIONS
Do not discuss clients in public areas, on social media, or with family and friends. Keep phones silenced and do not photograph clients or their information. Report any suspected breach to your supervisor or Privacy Officer immediately.

PRIVACY OFFICER
The Administrator serves as the agency Privacy Officer. All staff receive HIPAA training upon hire and annually. Violations may result in disciplinary action.

steps.title: Hour 2: Cultural Sensitivity & Diversity
steps.content:
WHY DIVERSITY MATTERS
Our clients and team come from many backgrounds. Cultural awareness helps us communicate clearly, build trust, and deliver person-centered care that respects each individual.

DIMENSIONS OF DIVERSITY
Diversity includes race, ethnicity, language, religion, age, ability, gender, sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, and nationality. Each dimension shapes how a person sees the world.

AVOID ASSUMPTIONS
Do not assume a client believes, eats, prays, or communicates the way you do. Ask respectful questions and listen to the answers. What is polite in one culture may be different in another.

LANGUAGE AND COMMUNICATION
Speak clearly and simply. A client's limited English does not reflect intelligence. Use interpreters or translated materials when needed. Do not rely on family members to interpret sensitive information unless approved.

RESPECTING BELIEFS AND PRACTICES
Honor religious practices, dietary preferences, modesty needs, and family roles. Schedule care around important practices when possible and respectfully ask what matters to the client.

BUILDING CULTURAL AWARENESS
Admit what you do not know, suspend judgment, practice empathy, check your assumptions, and celebrate differences. Cultural competence grows with curiosity and respect.
